item.title: Europe gripped by cost-of-living turmoil
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
Europe gripped by cost-of-living turmoil People throughout the continent take to the streets to protest against rising prices, reduced purchasing power The wave of protests and unrest that swept through France and several other European countries in recent days may soon subside, but the economic pressure and widespread frustration that caused it remain. For Laurent Mazzarolo, a train driver living in Paris, the demonstrations reflect the growing difficulty ordinary people face in maintaining their living standards, as prices rise and purchasing power weakens. "Ten years ago, you could live quite comfortably on a salary of 2,000 euros ($2,247) a month. Now, even with 3,000 euros, life can be quite difficult, especially in Paris," he said. "Before, you could go to a restaurant four or five times a month. Now, maybe once or twice, or sometimes not at all. People have less money to enjoy themselves, and that means less social interaction," he said. Even with a stable job, Mazzarolo said he struggles to balance his monthly expenses, despite cutting back on leisure spending, and that makes him particularly concerned about people in younger generations, who face difficulties in securing a place at their preferred university and in pursuing the careers they want. "They cannot imagine their future," he said. "I can understand why people are frustrated about the cost of living, but I don't like the way it's being expressed through violence. For me, that's not the right way." Similar concerns are being voiced in Madrid, where the rising cost of housing has left young people worried about the prospect of living independently. Rocio, an 18-year-old student who lives with her parents and brother, said she joined a protest because she fears she may eventually be unable to afford a home of her own. "The prices just keep on getting higher, and I know by the time I can live on my own, they will be even higher," she said. Richard, a Frenchman living in Brussels, Belgium, has similar fears. "Today, when I go to (the supermarket) to buy three items, say a pack of milk and some cereal, I pay 15 euros," he said. "If you're a parent, the question arises: how can you teach your children that quality matters, and what values are you truly able to pass on? Ultimately, for someone like me in a comfortable income bracket, the question comes down to one word: dignity. Can you live with dignity when you work? That is, can your work enable you to pay your bills and provide for your children's needs, while still looking at life with some sense of hope, rather than being driven solely by day-to-day necessity?" Economic indicators illustrate the situation. According to Eurostat data, annual inflation in the area that uses the euro for currency rose to 3.8 percent in September, after having been 3.2 percent in August. Energy prices increased in September by 18.8 percent year-on-year, after having been 14.3 percent the previous month. The high cost of energy is widely believed to add disproportionate pressure to lower-income households, leaving them less money for food, healthcare, education, and housing. Rising rent According to Deutsche Bank Research Institute's report Mapping the World's Prices 2026, a household with two earners receiving average local net salaries in Lisbon, Portugal, would have just 253 euros left each month after renting a three-bedroom apartment in the city center, which is the smallest amount of disposable income recorded among 28 European cities surveyed. The pressure is also evident in Brussels, where the average monthly rent for newly signed leases through real estate agencies rose from 1,113 euros in 2021 to 1,376 euros in 2025, according to the CIB-Korfine Rental Barometer. That represents an increase of approximately 23.6 percent in four years, adding 263 euros to the average monthly rental bill for newly contracted properties. Yan Xiaoxiao, an associate researcher at the Institute of International Relations at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, who is conducting research in Europe, said the protests across the continent point to a common economic dilemma. "With economic growth slowing, governments are finding it increasingly difficult to meet public expectations for living standards and social protection," he said. "On the one hand, people expect governments to improve public services and provide more public goods to ease the pressure on their daily lives. On the other hand, governments are under pressure to reduce fiscal deficits." Yan noted that the current wave of protests has involved people from different age groups and occupations, reflecting discontent that extends beyond any single section of society. Past protests have tended to attract participants from specific sections of society. "The latest unrest can be seen as an expression of dissatisfaction that has accumulated since its last breakout," he said. "I paid 18.50 euros for a tube of eye ointment and 11.50 euros for a simple meal at McDonald's," Yan said. "I can't imagine my financial pressure if I were to live here for a long time." Li Zhengdong, an associate professor at the Institute of Central and Eastern European Studies at Ningbo University, who is on an academic tour in Europe, noted: "The real test facing Europe today is not simply whether governments can contain street violence, but whether they can prevent mounting socioeconomic tensions from escalating into divisions between different social groups and, ultimately, a political crisis." Back in Paris, Mazzarolo said he suspects "the government is doing what it can, but not enough". He said policymakers should strive to be "closer to the people" and "act like normal people". "Sometimes, we have the feeling that politicians are living on another planet," he said. "Even if you don't have the solutions, at least show more empathy." Asked what he expects the government to do after the protests end, 22-year-old Jorge Salas in Madrid replied: "Right now, nothing. For years, we haven't received a real answer or any meaningful help. The demonstrations are about more than housing costs. They also reflect concerns over education, access to public services, and the opportunities available to ordinary people." Salas pointed to the financial burden the purchase of schoolbooks places on low-income families, saying that providing children with a good education should be a government priority. "We need books, we need food, we need help to buy a house and start a family," he said. "We are not simply asking for a better life. We are asking for a chance to improve our lives." Huang Xiaodi contributed to the story. Contact the writers at zhangzhouxiang@chinadaily.com.cn.

item.title: Xi urges drawing on Long March spirit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Xi urges drawing on Long March spirit Long March: High-quality development emphasized Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, called on Thursday for drawing strength from the Long March spirit to overcome difficulties, tackle risks and meet challenges, and to ensure that the giant ship of China's national rejuvenation cuts through the waves and sails steadily forward, as the country marked the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March. Addressing a gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, Xi linked the revolutionary journey nine decades ago to China's current pursuit of national rejuvenation, describing the drive to build China into a great modern socialist country in all respects, and to advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization, as a new Long March for the Party and the people. Xi, who is also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that revisiting history is about drawing wisdom and strength from it to forge ahead. He described the Long March, a strategic military maneuver carried out by the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army of the CPC from 1934 to 1936, as an earthshaking revolutionary feat of great significance in the history of the Party, the country and the military, with a profound impact on the path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. "This stirring heroic epic will forever be engraved on the monument of the Chinese revolution and remembered in the hearts of hundreds of millions of people," he said. The Red Army traversed more than 10 provinces on a 12,500-kilometer journey and broke through encirclement and pursuit by more than a million enemy troops, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said. At his proposal, participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China. Reflecting on the path to the Long March victory, Xi highlighted the Party's correct leadership, firm revolutionary conviction, independence and a commitment to seeking truth from facts, as well as the support of the people. He emphasized the need to integrate the basic tenets of Marxism into China's specific realities, and to remain deeply rooted in the people, whom he described as the enduring source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces. The great spirit of the Long March, demonstrating the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity, will always be a precious treasure and a powerful source of inspiration for overcoming difficulties and forging ahead, Xi said. Over the past 90 years, the Party has united and led the people through one great Long March after another during revolution, construction and reform, achieving one great victory after another, he said. Xi said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the second centenary goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said. Setting out the tasks ahead, Xi called for upholding the Party's ideals, convictions and fundamental purpose, remaining true to its original aspiration and founding mission, and relying closely on the people to make further historic achievements. He stressed the need to pursue high-quality development, better meet people's growing aspirations for a better life, and promote common prosperity for all. Economic development must deliver both improvements in quality and reasonable growth in quantity, he said. Xi also called for better coordination between development and security, and for taking the initiative to overcome difficulties, address risks and meet challenges. On national defense, he urged faster progress toward building world-class armed forces, upholding the Party's absolute leadership over the military, achieving the military's centenary goals on schedule, and advancing high-quality modernization of national defense and the armed forces. He further emphasized upholding Party leadership and strengthening Party building, with sustained efforts to exercise full and rigorous Party self-governance and enhance the Party's capacity to purify, improve and renew itself and excel.

item.title: Shenzhen, a high-tech city serving people
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Shenzhen, a high-tech city serving people Share - WeChat
Many people's first impression would be that Shenzhen, one of China's innovation hubs, resembles a cyberpunk-style city. But is that true? Cyberpunk is all about "high tech, low life". In those stories, there are gleaming, towering skyscrapers, and beneath them, cyborgs live in dark, chaotic, poverty-stricken neighborhoods. British vlogger Toby Symonds and China Daily reporter Yan An recently experienced the everyday life of residents in the city, and Toby's impression of Shenzhen has completely changed. Toby said that the technology in Shenzhen is not as cold as portrayed in movies and games, but rather has a warmth to it, truly serving people's lives. Watch the video to learn more.

item.title: China-Europe freight train service marks milestone
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
China-Europe freight train service marks milestone A China-Europe freight train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, Liaoning province, at 11:30 am on Thursday, bringing the service's cumulative trips to top 140,000 and transporting goods worth more than $560 billion since the rail network began operating in 2011. The milestone was achieved a decade after the service adopted the unified brand of China Railway Express in June 2016. According to China State Railway Group, the national railway operator, the network now connects 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries. An average of 51.2 China-Europe freight trains departed China daily through six major border crossings this year, up 12.8 percent year-on-year, the operator said. Freight flows have also become more balanced. In September, the ratio of return trips to outbound trips exceeded 90 percent for the ninth consecutive month. Vehicles and auto parts, machinery, and electrical and electronic products are among the major items of outbound cargo, while timber, pulp, agricultural products and consumer goods from Europe travel in the opposite direction. As the network expands, efforts are underway to make services more predictable and better suited to different types of cargo, helping businesses plan shipments and meet delivery commitments. A Moscow-bound train carrying auto parts, industrial machinery and precision instruments departed Beijing on Thursday. At Beijing International Land Port in Fangshan district, scheduled trains leave for Central Asia every Monday and for Europe every Thursday, supplemented by additional trains to meet demand. "With trains following a regular schedule, companies can book space ahead of time and plan when to make and ship their goods," said Sun Zhiyu, deputy general manager of the port. According to China Railway Beijing Group, scheduled China-Europe and China-Central Asia services from Beijing take about 12 to 15 days. Fixed departure times, routes and train numbers give businesses a more predictable delivery window. For Sinopec Lubricant Co, the rail connection is close to home, with its factory situated just over 10 kilometers from the inland port. Goods make the short trip to the port before continuing overseas by train. Sun said the company previously faced high transshipment costs and fluctuating transit times when exporting by sea. Using the rail service has significantly reduced its overall logistics costs and strengthened its confidence in expanding exports. International freight trains have made more than 100 trips from Beijing, according to China Railway Beijing Group. Destinations included Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan. Across the wider China-Europe network, 22 services with fixed timetables for their entire journeys operate each week between nine Chinese cities and six European cities. The national operator said predictable transit times help meet the cross-border shipping needs of high-end manufacturers. Innovation highlighted In Northeast China, growing vehicle exports have prompted another innovation: increasing the number of cars that can be loaded into each container while retaining its suitability for return journeys. Fan Zeyu, an operations management staff member at the Shenyang branch of China Railway Container Transport Co, said a new 40-foot container designed for vehicle shipments was first put to use in Changchun, Jilin province, in June. The container has 10 percent more usable internal space than a standard container and is fitted with folding vehicle racks. It can carry four cars or small and medium-sized sport utility vehicles, one more than a general-purpose container. Vehicles are loaded and secured outside the container before being moved inside. Each vehicle takes an average of just 15 minutes to load. "Customers told us the logistics cost per vehicle was 15 percent lower compared with exports by road," Fan said. Operational improvements are also helping speed up cross-border transport. The national operator has worked with customs authorities and overseas railway companies to streamline border procedures, reducing the time for customs clearance to less than 30 minutes in some cases. The operator said it will continue expanding capacity and improving services with overseas partners, with a focus on achieving a better balance between outbound and return traffic.

item.title: Shanghai studio brings Chinese icons to the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Hyper-realistic statues draw on pop culture, mythology to tell compelling stories Standing in front of a Bruce Lee statue at Infinity Studio in Shanghai, you might feel as if you had traveled through time and space to meet the real person. With a determined gaze, a touch of stubble, a natural expression, soft skin and smoothly defined muscles, the hyper-realistic, life-size silicone bust of the legendary martial artist looks absolutely lifelike. Striving for ultimate authenticity, the team even used human hair implantation techniques to create the statue's eyelashes, eyebrows and hair. Even the stubble was implanted and then shaved to achieve the most realistic appearance possible, according to Yu Guanglai, the founder of Infinity Studio. "Bruce Lee is arguably one of the most influential figures in the entire overseas Chinese community. He truly introduced Chinese kung fu to the whole world, and we want to preserve and present the best of him," Yu said. His words reflect the studio's commitment to "portraying the Chinese". With the statues, the team hopes to make more Chinese heroes and stories known to the world. In 2017, the team delved deeper into traditional Chinese culture and launched its Chinese mythology series, and the notable heroic characters Nezha, Yang Jian and the Monkey King took on a life of their own in the team's hands. Yu used to be a collector of statues and figures. More than a decade ago, he was eager to buy products from Chinese franchises, but could barely find any on the market. After 3D printing technology entered the consumer market, Yu and his partners founded the studio in 2015. Their first original series was inspired by the Chinese historical epic Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Released in stages starting in 2016, the 1/4 scale statue series quickly became a hit not only in China, but also among Southeast Asian enthusiasts who share similar cultural roots. Yu also highlighted the studio's 12 Chinese zodiac animal sculptures, a series based on the original full-body statues at Yuanmingyuan (Old Summer Palace), of which only the iconic animal heads survive today. The studio holds a number of major licenses for iconic global franchises, including DC Comics, The Lord of the Rings, Avatar, World of Warcraft and League of Legends. Among them, 1,000 preorders of the world's first life-size silicone bust of Wonder Woman, a character from DC Entertainment's Justice League, sold out globally within one hour in 2019. China's pop toy industry is projected to reach 110.1 billion yuan ($16.5 billion) by 2026, with an average annual growth rate of over 20 percent, according to a report on China's pop toy and animation and comic industries released by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' National Academy of Economic Strategy. "China's complete and efficient supply chain is essential for all statue makers seeking competitive products," said Peng Jiongyun, Infinity Studio's head of marketing. In recent years, China's figure and statue market has flourished. Early this month, the annual Shanghai Wonder Festival, hosted by Chinese video-sharing platform Bilibili, gathered over 100,000 products and drew more than 150,000 visitors, along with over 400 business exhibitors and more than 2,700 individual exhibitors from around the world. Peng said that Infinity Studio's team has witnessed rapidly growing demand for products derived from more domestic works, such as A Record of a Mortal's Journey to Immortality and Wuthering Waves. Many other companies are also looking beyond traditional toy models, including Jizai, based in Xiamen, Fujian province. Aiming to showcase the beauty of nature and metal craftsmanship through Eastern aesthetics, the company uses metallic materials rather than traditional resin to make traditional heroic figures. Chen Ye, founder of Jizai, said, "We hope people from diverse cultural backgrounds can experience our exquisite metal works and forge a connection with Chinese culture." wangxin2@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: DPP slammed for betraying nation, history
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
DPP slammed for betraying nation, history The Chinese mainland has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities for barring people on the island from attending an event scheduled on the mainland in November to mark the 160th birth anniversary of Sun Yat-sen, saying the move betrays the nation and its history. Sun, a founding figure of the Chinese Kuomintang party and a revered revolutionary leader, died in 1925 in Beijing. His remains rest at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu province. The commemorative event aims to carry forward Sun's noble spirit of upholding national unity and striving for national rejuvenation, Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday. The event aims to unite all Chinese people, including Taiwan compatriots, in opposing "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference and in promoting cross-Strait exchanges and integration, she added. Recently, Taiwan's "mainland affairs council" claimed that the commemoration would promote the idea of "anti-'independence' and pro-reunification". For the first time, it issued an explicit ban on participation in the event, saying that it would deny permission to anyone wanting to travel to the mainland to attend the commemoration, including county and city heads. Zhang, the mainland spokeswoman, accused the DPP authorities of resorting to every possible means to obstruct and restrict cross-Strait exchanges while intimidating and suppressing people in Taiwan. The decision "exposes the vicious intentions" of the DPP authorities "to obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and suppress Taiwan compatriots, betray the nation and history, split the country and stoke confrontation across the Taiwan Strait", Zhang said. "Their actions will inevitably meet with opposition and condemnation from all Chinese people," she added. Despite the DPP authorities' efforts to decouple the island's industries from the mainland market, latest statistics show robust growth in cross-Strait trade and people-to-people exchanges. In September, the value of Taiwan's exports to the mainland reached $20.6 billion, up 30.2 percent year-on-year, while its imports from the mainland totaled $13.5 billion, up 59.1 percent year-on-year, according to data released by Taiwan's finance department. According to the General Administration of Customs, the value of cross-Strait trade reached $301.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 30.3 percent year-on-year. The mainland's exports to Taiwan totaled $84.9 billion, up 37.3 percent, while its imports from Taiwan reached $216.3 billion, up 27.8 percent. Zhang said these figures demonstrate that cross-Strait industrial and supply chains remain stable and strong, and that markets on both sides of the Strait will never be decoupled, adding that economic exchanges and shared development across the Strait are an unstoppable trend. She emphasized that the DPP's moves to obstruct cross-Strait economic exchanges and cooperation and push for decoupling of supply chains to serve external forces are doomed to fail. Despite the DPP's standing travel curbs, 2.49 million trips by Taiwan residents to the mainland were recorded from January to August, up 19.6 percent year-on-year, according to data released by Taiwan authorities. Noting that attempts to prevent Taiwan residents from visiting the mainland are "absurd and futile", the spokeswoman urged the DPP authorities to abandon political maneuvering, withdraw unreasonable restrictions and facilitate cultural exchanges across the Strait. According to media reports, the DPP authorities have rejected an application by mainland actor Zhang Linghe, who has gained popularity in Taiwan for his drama Pursuit of Jade, to hold a fan meeting on the island. In response, the spokeswoman criticized the DPP for politicizing cross-Strait cultural exchanges, obstructing people-to-people interactions and disregarding public sentiment.

item.title: Long March memories live on through village traditions
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
Long March memories live on through village traditions in Gansu Ninety years ago, during the Long March, the First and Fourth Front Armies of the Red Army joined forces in Huining county, Gansu province. In the county's Hongbuzi village, residents provided the soldiers with grain and other supplies. The soldiers left IOUs for the grain they took, promising to repay the villagers after the revolution — a gesture that reflected the Red Army's emphasis on maintaining close ties with the people. That memory has been passed down through generations in Hongbuzi, where the Long March spirit of relying on and supporting the people remains part of the local heritage. In neighboring Tuoying village, residents have brought the story to life through a modern Qinqiang Opera performance, using a traditional Chinese theatrical form to share the history with new audiences. Since June 2021, the local folk orchestra has staged 116 performances, reaching an audience of 289,000. As gongs and drums ring out onstage, the story of the Red Army and its ties with local communities continues to reach new generations.

item.title: 'China Haul': Empty suitcases in, packed suitcases out
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
When a British woman suffering from hindered mobility following a stroke was able to discard her wheelchair and walk with the help of a Chinese-made exoskeleton robot at the China Import and Export Fair this week, she could barely hold back her tears. Her son, who was equally overwhelmed by what Chinese technology could achieve, decided to immediately place an order for the device. "I have never seen anything like this in the United Kingdom, or even in Europe," he said. The heartwarming moment was captured on camera, and the footage was widely circulated on social media. Rafael Saavedra, a Venezuelan vlogger attending the fair, described the scene as a glimpse into the future. "Here you can see, touch and test tomorrow's consumer technology — from robots that can run errands to massage chairs," he said. The scene was actually far from unique, as the viral "China Haul" trend has gripped the ongoing China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, which opened in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, on Oct 14 and runs through Nov 4. While influencers have popularized the "China Haul" hashtag on social media, visitors to the fair are buyers searching for China's next-generation products. Across the fair's exhibition halls, foreign visitors were captivated by artificial intelligence-based toys, humanoid robots and other smart devices, with some placing orders on the spot. Their shopping lists tell a broader story. After last year's boom in "China Travel" brought millions of overseas visitors to the country, the latest trend indicates that many are returning home with something more than intangible memories. They are packing their suitcases with Chinese brands — from tech products such as drones and foldable smartphones to lifestyle goods such as sports shoes and AI-powered toys. In other words, China's appeal is moving beyond affordability toward innovation, and that momentum is reflected in official figures. China recorded 23.72 million visa-free entries by foreign nationals from January to August, up 26.8 percent year-on-year, according to the National Immigration Administration. Data from the Ministry of Commerce shows that in the first seven months, overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan ($39.5 billion), an increase of 27.8 percent compared with the same period a year earlier. It underscores a steady recovery in inbound tourism and consumer spending. Speaking on Friday at a news conference in Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said that China will continue opening its doors wider, allowing more foreign visitors to better understand and appreciate the country through two-way exchanges. The growing enthusiasm for "China Haul" among visitors is also benefiting international retailers. According to Inditex, a global fashion retailer that owns brands including Zara and Massimo Dutti, the share of sales generated by overseas visitors at the Zara flagship store on Shanghai's Nanjing East Road and the Massimo Dutti store on Nanjing West Road has risen more than 10 percent year-on-year. The company attributed the increase in sales to the stores' central locations, the distinctive shopping experiences they offer, their assortment of products, and China's increasingly convenient departure tax refund policy. Taikoo Li, a popular commercial zone in Beijing's Sanlitun, reported a similar trend. The retail complex said the city's continued efforts to improve services for visitors, streamline tax refund procedures and enhance cultural and tourism experiences are attracting more foreigners. "The number of overseas visitors to our complex has seen a clear upward trend," said CT Ma, general manager of Taikoo Li Sanlitun. "International shoppers are interested not only in global luxury brands, but also in Chinese brands that combine local cultural elements with contemporary design. Sportswear, lifestyle products and brands with distinctive Chinese characteristics have become particularly popular," he said. "They are no longer coming only to see China. They are coming to discover what China makes, what China designs and, increasingly, what China creates," Ma said.
